periods.activity_title: Entering the Garden-Painting: Reading and First Responses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.86): paired discussion on colours and sights in a garden
Reflect and Respond (p.87): acquaint with palette, hue, canvas; identify each in given painting
Check Your Understanding (p.88): select the appropriate stanza title from five options

homework.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.86): write two sentence-frame comparisons between a garden and a painting

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud while students follow in their textbooks (p.86–88), attending to rhythm and the garden-painting imagery. Students note any image or phrase that strikes them.
Reflect and Respond — paired exchange: students share what they see in a garden, the colours, and where they find them. A few pairs report to the class.
Reflect and Respond — teacher introduces the terms palette, hue, and canvas using the painting on p.87. Students identify each element in the painting and share orally.

Check Your Understanding — students work individually to match each stanza with its most fitting title from the five given options (p.88). Class discussion follows, with students justifying their choices by pointing to specific lines.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem builds an extended metaphor in which every gardening element — earth, seeds, plot — maps precisely onto a painting element; drawing out this mapping early gives students the conceptual frame they need for closer work. Students may initially overlook the allegorical layer (the garden as life's journey, the gardener as anyone cultivating beauty through effort) — prompt them with 'What might the gardener stand for beyond someone who grows plants?' The task on identifying palette, hue, and canvas in a visual serves as a concrete bridge before the abstract language of the poem.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for listing garden colours

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Devices, Extracts, and Deeper Meanings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.88–89): match poetic devices to examples; discuss in pairs
Critical Reflection (p.89–91): extract-based questions on 'Brushstrokes of seeds' and 'Each plot, a canvas wide'

homework.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.91): four sentence-completion comparisons — painter/gardener, palette/earth, brushstrokes/seeds, canvas/plot

time_bands.activity: Brief re-reading of the poem (p.86–88) by students silently, keeping the garden-painting conceit in mind before moving to device identification.

Reading for Appreciation (p.88–89) — pairs match the seven poetic devices (imagery, metaphor, rhyme scheme, tone, mood, speaker, alliteration) to their examples in the poem. Pairs share and resolve disagreements through whole-class discussion.

Critical Reflection (p.89–91) — teacher works through both extract sets with the class. For Extract 1 ('Brushstrokes of seeds, planted true'), students tackle the metaphor-identification, 'planted true' significance, word-choice of 'hue', the analogy, and the assertion–reason item. For Extract 2 ('Each plot, a canvas wide'), students address plot's referent, rhyme-scheme imitation, the line conveying aesthetic-natural blend, the canvas simile, and the word-choice of 'wide'. Each item is discussed before moving on.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem as a whole in the opening unit, students now encounter it at the level of individual word choices and structural devices; invite them to read each extract aloud before answering to re-activate the sound of the poem. The alliteration example 'Blossoms bloom' is easy to spot, but the distinction between tone (appreciative) and mood (joyful) is frequently confused at secondary — pause there and ask students to articulate the difference in their own words. The assertion–reason item on gardeners waiting for spring benefits from a two-step approach: verify assertion and reason separately, then judge the explanatory link.
materials: Blackboard for mapping device names to examples

periods.activity_title: Colour Language and Garden Voices: Vocabulary Then Listening

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.92): explore shade names for green, red, blue; pair discussion on associations
Vocabulary in Context (p.92): art-studio paragraph — contextual prediction of easel, portrait, mural, tonal range, underpainting
Listen and Respond (p.93): listen once; identify which of three items the girl does NOT mention
Listen and Respond (p.93–94): listen again; circle correct answers for seven detail questions

time_bands.activity: Vocabulary in Context — teacher reads aloud the lists of shade names for blue, red, and green (p.92). Pairs choose two shades and share the things they associate with each, using the discussion frame provided.

Vocabulary in Context — teacher reads the art-studio paragraph (p.92) while students follow. Pairs predict the meanings of the five underlined painting-related words using the sentence frame 'I think ______ means ______ because the passage talks about ______.' Pairs share predictions; teacher confirms.
Listen and Respond — first listening: teacher reads the transcript (p.264) or plays the audio. Students identify which of the three pictured items the girl does not talk about and share answers.

Listen and Respond — second listening: teacher reads the transcript again. Students circle the correct answer for each of the seven detail questions about flower colours, plant positions, evergreen count, brick paint colours, central tree, and waste-material creations (p.93–94). Answers are verified as a class.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary work on shade names connects directly to the poem's visual imagery — encouraging students to notice, for instance, that 'crimson' and 'scarlet' carry different intensities deepens their appreciation of why the poet chose 'shades of green, red, and blue' rather than listing specific shades. The listening passage describes a school garden in precise spatial terms (left corners, right corners, centre), so students may find it helpful to sketch a rough layout as they listen — this is a legitimate comprehension strategy to suggest. The distinction between items the girl mentions in passing (butterflies, bench) and items she does not mention (garden hose) rewards careful listening rather than inference.
materials: Transcript p.264 (teacher copy) or audio playback device
Blank paper for optional garden-layout sketches

periods.activity_title: Expressing Preferences and Exploring Gardens Beyond the Page

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.94): note advantages of flower and vegetable gardens for homes
Speaking Activity (p.94): paired turn-taking — state and justify preference using four sentence prompts
Learning Beyond the Text (p.95–96): introduce mini-project; students choose two assignments and plan their inquiry

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.96): read Toru Dutt's 'A Sea of Foliage Girds Our Garden Round'; note one image that strikes you

time_bands.activity: Speaking Activity — individually, students think and note down at least two advantages each of a flower garden and a vegetable garden as home gardens (p.94). Teacher circulates and prompts students who need support.

Speaking Activity — paired turn-taking: each student states and justifies their preference (flower or vegetable garden) using all four sentence prompts in rotation (p.94). Partners listen and respond with agreement or reasoned disagreement. Selected pairs share with the class.

Learning Beyond the Text — teacher introduces the mini-project (p.95–96), reads each of the four assignment options aloud, and explains that students must select one from options 1–2 and one from options 3–4. Students read the options, ask questions, and write a brief plan (two or three bullet points) for each chosen assignment in their notebooks.

Two or three students share which assignments they have chosen and one question they plan to investigate. Teacher closes with a brief reminder to read Toru Dutt's poem at home and note a striking image.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task builds on the poem's celebration of gardens as places of beauty and purpose — students who have engaged with the garden-as-canvas metaphor may find themselves arguing for flower gardens on aesthetic grounds, while others lean toward vegetable gardens on practical ones; both positions are equally valid and the sentence frames are designed to make either defensible. For the mini-project, ensure that each student has a clear, written two-line plan before leaving; a vague intention rarely produces sustained inquiry over several weeks. The Toru Dutt poem assigned as self-reading offers a compelling contrast — her garden is lush, overwhelming, and rooted in an Indian landscape — and students who notice this contrast are already practising the comparative reading the project may call for.
materials: Notebooks and pens for noting advantages and project plans

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, extended metaphor, and word-choice effects using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Extended garden-painting metaphor in Maya Anthony's twelve-line AABB poem.
items.item_stem: In 'Canvas of Soil', Maya Anthony writes: 'Palette of earth, rich and deep, / Where dreams of gardeners seep.' Which statement best explains what this opening metaphor suggests about the relationship between a garden and a painter's palette?

options.label: A
options.text: The earth is compared to a palette because both are oval or rectangular in shape.

options.label: B
options.text: The earth, like a palette, holds a rich variety of raw materials from which the gardener creates something beautiful.

options.label: C
options.text: The gardener's dreams seep into the earth the way paint seeps into a canvas when it is left in the rain.

options.label: D
options.text: The metaphor suggests that gardening is more difficult than painting because soil is harder to work with than paint.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has noticed the visual comparison but conflated the shape of a palette with the metaphor's actual meaning about creative potential.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has taken 'seep' too literally and applied it to the paint rather than reading 'dreams of gardeners seep' as aspirations nourishing the soil.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has inverted the poem's tone, reading difficulty where the poem expresses celebratory ease and creative abundance.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, extended metaphor, and word-choice effects using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Extended garden-painting metaphor in Maya Anthony's twelve-line AABB poem.
items.item_stem:
Read the third stanza on p.88, beginning "Each plot, a canvas wide,". Then answer the questions below.

1. The stanza says art and life 'coincide' in each garden plot. What does this word choice reveal about the poet's view of the relationship between creativity and the natural world?
2. The final line, 'Gardens become paintings still', uses the word 'still' ambiguously. Identify both meanings the word carries here and explain how each meaning supports the poem's central idea.
3. Considering the poem as a whole, evaluate how effectively the extended metaphor of garden-as-painting sustains itself across all three stanzas. Support your response with at least two examples from the poem.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the third stanza on p.88, beginning "Each plot, a canvas wide,".

expected_elements: 1. 'Coincide' implies art and life are not separate; creativity is inherent in natural growth.
2. 'Still' as 'motionless': gardens frozen as paintings; as 'even now': nature's beauty endures forever.
3. Metaphor is consistent: palette→earth, brushstrokes→seeds, canvas→plot throughout.
Credit examples from any two of the three stanzas to support the evaluation.
Higher marks for noting the allegorical layer: the gardener as anyone cultivating beauty through effort.

items.source_context: A girl's oral description of her school garden's layout, plants, and decorated features.
items.item_stem:
A student describes her school garden. Listen carefully and decide whether each statement below is true or false. Write T or F next to each statement.
(1) The first row of flowers in the garden is red.
(2) The Nature Club members painted the border bricks white and red.
(3) The banyan tree stands at the entrance of the garden.
(4) The Art and Craft Club created scarecrows and pinwheels from waste materials.

options.text: The Art and Craft Club created scarecrows and pinwheels from waste materials.
The banyan tree stands at the entrance of the garden.
The first row of flowers in the garden is red.
The Nature Club members painted the border bricks white and red.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — F (the first row has pink flowers, not red); 2 — T (the Nature Club painted the border bricks white and red); 3 — F (the banyan tree stands in the centre, not at the entrance; the bench is near the entrance); 4 — T (the Art and Craft Club made scarecrows, pinwheels, and dustbins from waste materials).

items.source_lo: Student identifies specific details and omissions from a spoken description using focused listening.
items.source_context: A girl's oral description of her school garden's layout, plants, and decorated features.
items.item_stem: After listening to the girl's description of her school garden, answer in one or two sentences: What impression of the school community does the description create, and which two specific details from the garden best support that impression?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The description creates an impression of a caring, creative school community that takes pride in its surroundings. This is supported by details such as the Nature Club members painting the border bricks and the Art and Craft Club making decorative items like scarecrows and pinwheels from waste materials.

items.item_stem: Describe, in about one minute of speech, one clear advantage of having a flower garden at home and one clear advantage of having a vegetable garden at home. Use at least one of the following sentence frames: 'A flower garden is valuable because…'; 'On the other hand, a vegetable garden offers…'

expected_elements: Names one specific advantage of a flower garden (e.g. aesthetic beauty, colour, fragrance).
Names one specific advantage of a vegetable garden (e.g. fresh produce, self-sufficiency, economy).
Uses at least one of the given sentence frames correctly.
Speaks in complete sentences with adequate volume and clarity.

items.source_context: Choosing between a flower garden and a vegetable garden for a home, with stated reasons.
items.item_stem: Your partner has just argued that a vegetable garden is the better choice for a home because it is practical and economical. Respond by arguing for a flower garden instead. State at least two reasons, anticipate one counter-argument your partner might raise, and address it. Speak for about ninety seconds.

expected_elements: States at least two distinct reasons favouring a flower garden.
Acknowledges the partner's practicality argument and offers a substantive response.
Uses logical connectives (however, on the other hand, nonetheless) to structure the rebuttal.
Maintains a courteous, reasoned tone throughout.
Sustains argument for approximately the stated duration without significant loss of coherence.

items.item_stem: Match each art-studio word in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| easel | the full range of light and dark tones in a painting |
| tonal range | a large painting made directly on a wall |
| portrait | a stand that holds a canvas upright while an artist paints |
| underpainting | a painting or drawing of a person's face or figure |
| mural | a first layer of paint applied to guide later colours and shading |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: easel — a stand that holds a canvas upright while an artist paints; tonal range — the full range of light and dark tones in a painting; portrait — a painting or drawing of a person's face or figure; underpainting — a first layer of paint applied to guide later colours and shading; mural — a large painting made directly on a wall.

the full range of light and dark tones in a painting
a painting or drawing of a person's face or figure

items.item_stem:
The poem 'Canvas of Soil' mentions 'shades of green, red, and blue'. For each sentence below, replace the underlined general colour word with the most fitting specific shade from the box, and briefly explain your choice in a few words.

Box: scarlet · cobalt blue · olive · crimson · sky blue · pistachio

(a) The roses at the garden's edge glowed a deep, intense red (underlined: red) in the afternoon sun.
(b) The gardener painted the old wooden bench a calm, light blue (underlined: blue) to match the open sky above.
(c) The hardy low shrubs were a muted, earthy green (underlined: green) that blended with the dry soil.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) crimson or scarlet — both denote intense, deep red; crimson is slightly darker and suits roses in strong light; scarlet is brighter. Either is acceptable with a reasonable explanation. (b) sky blue — a calm, light blue that evokes open sky, matching the sentence context. (c) olive — a muted, earthy greenish-brown shade that blends naturally with dry soil.

items.source_context: Gardens as designed spaces of cultural significance, artistic inspiration, and living craftsmanship.
items.item_stem: Choose ONE famous Indian garden (such as Amrit Udyan, Brindavan Gardens, or any other you know). Write a short paragraph (five to seven sentences) describing its most striking design feature and explaining what that feature reveals about the cultural values or aesthetic traditions it was built to express.

expected_elements: Names a specific Indian garden and one clearly identified design feature.
Connects the feature to a cultural value or aesthetic tradition with a stated reason.
Demonstrates basic awareness that gardens are designed, not accidental.
Writes in five to seven coherent sentences with accurate grammar.
Avoids generic statements; grounds the response in the chosen garden's actual characteristics.

items.source_lo: Student investigates a theme through independent inquiry, connecting a poem's world to cultural and interdisciplinary contexts.
items.source_context: Gardens as designed spaces of cultural significance, artistic inspiration, and living craftsmanship.
items.item_stem:
Design and present a Garden Inquiry Project. Choose TWO of the following four assignments — one from the first pair (A or B) and one from the second pair (C or D) — and complete both.

A. Research any five famous gardens of India, focusing on their history, design elements, and cultural significance. Prepare a short written report and an oral presentation.
B. Find a well-known painting or sculpture inspired by a garden. Analyse how the garden is represented and create your own visual or written response inspired by it.
C. Design your own garden on paper or using a digital tool. Label key design choices and artistic influences, and present your decisions to the class.
D. Interview a local gardener or landscaping expert. Prepare questions about practical gardening or landscaping, conduct the interview, and write a summary of what you learned.

Your submission should demonstrate research, personal analysis, and clear communication.

expected_elements: Completes two assignments: one from A/B and one from C/D, both with evidence of genuine inquiry.
Shows research depth: specific names, dates, or facts, not only general observations.
Includes personal analysis or creative response, not only description or summary.
Communicates findings clearly — written, visual, or oral — in appropriate form for the assignment.
Connects findings to the poem's theme of gardens as spaces where art and life coincide.
